[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in local labor markets with high employer concentration (e.g., using Herfindahl-Hirschman Index thresholds) and tight labor conditions, focusing on employment outcomes for low-skilled workers. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing employment changes in high-monopsony tight markets vs. competitive markets, isolating the predicted hiring effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural estimation of labor supply elasticities and firm-level wage-setting models under monopsony, calibrated to tight labor market data. — Validates the proposed mechanism (monopsony power reduction) and identifies the wage threshold where the effect reverses, providing formal conditions for the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing minimum wage studies that stratify results by labor market tightness and employer concentration indices. — Synthesizes prior evidence to assess whether the predicted pattern holds across multiple contexts, clarifying the disputed status and confidence level.

scope.domain: tight labor markets characterized by employer concentration and limited worker mobility

qualifier.threshold: effect reverses above competitive wage equilibrium

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C006.object: unemployment among low-skilled workers in tight labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage unemployment among low-skilled workers in tight labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) minimum wage study (New Jersey-Pennsylvania fast-food restaurant panel) re-analyzed with modern causal inference methods (e.g., synthetic control or difference-in-differences with tight labor market stratification) — This classic natural experiment directly examined minimum wage effects on low-skilled employment in a tight labor market. Re-analyzing with updated methods and focusing on post-2000 data can confirm or refute whether the original findings of no negative employment effects hold under modern conditions and low substitution elasticity.

[PATH:literature] Cengiz et al. (2019) 'The Effect of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Jobs' (Quarterly Journal of Economics) — subgroup analysis for tight labor markets (low unemployment rate states/metro areas) — This comprehensive study uses a bunching estimator across many U.S. minimum wage changes. Extracting results specifically for tight labor markets (e.g., unemployment < 4%) and low substitution elasticity industries (e.g., retail, food service) would directly test the hypothesis's scope condition.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulated structural labor market model with heterogeneous agents and low substitution elasticity (calibrated to U.S. post-2000 data) — A computational model can isolate the mechanism: in tight labor markets with low substitution elasticity, firms may absorb wage increases via reduced profits or price pass-through rather than layoffs. Simulating counterfactual minimum wage hikes while varying elasticity parameters would provide theoretical confirmation or refutation of the hypothesis.

scope.domain: tight labor markets with low substitution elasticity

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with monopsony power and low worker mobility
C007.object: labor force participation by up to 8% among workers aged 25-54 without college degrees, with strongest effects in the first 18 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with monopsony power and low worker mobility labor force participation by up to 8% among workers aged 25-54 without college degrees, with strongest effects in the first 18 months]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. counties with high employer concentration (e.g., using Herfindahl-Hirschman Index > 0.25) and low cross-county commuting rates, analyzing CPS or ACS data for labor force participation of 25-54 year olds without college degrees. — Directly tests the hypothesis in the specified scope by leveraging variation in minimum wage policies across local monopsonistic labor markets, with panel data to capture 18-month dynamics and control for automation trends.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching labor market models incorporating monopsony power and endogenous automation decisions, calibrated to U.S. regional data with low worker mobility. — Provides a causal framework to assess whether the predicted 8% participation increase and 18-month peak are consistent with equilibrium effects, including firms' substitution toward automation after the initial adjustment period.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of minimum wage effects on labor force participation in monopsonistic settings, focusing on studies that measure employer concentration and mobility constraints (e.g., work by Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum). — Synthesizes existing empirical and theoretical evidence to evaluate whether the 8% effect size and temporal pattern are plausible given prior estimates, and identifies gaps in the evidence base for the specific demographic and market conditions.

scope.domain: regional labor markets with employer concentration ratios above 0.25 and limited geographic mobility

qualifier.temporal_dynamics: effects peak at 18 months then decline as firms adjust through automation
qualifier.mechanism: reduced search frictions and increased reservation wages under monopsony conditions

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of minimum wage effects on employment and participation, such as Doucouliagos & Stanley (2009) or more recent updates, stratified by labor market tightness and enforcement strength. — A systematic review of existing evidence across developed economies can reveal whether the predicted negative effects are robust in the specified contexts, and identify heterogeneity that confirms or refutes the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor supply models incorporating search frictions and firm monopsony power (e.g., Manning 2003; Dube et al. 2010), calibrated to post-2000 data from developed economies. — These models can simulate the mechanisms linking minimum wage to labor force participation and unemployment under varying demand conditions, providing a theoretical foundation to interpret empirical findings and test the hypothesis's underlying assumptions.

qualifier.geographic: developed economies with formal labor markets
